'''H. Jay Melosh''' (June 23, 1947 – September 11, 2020)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/h-jay-melosh-cwf2ae/|title=H. Jay Melosh}}</ref> was an American [[geophysicist]] specialising in [[impact crater]]ing. He earned a degree in physics from [[Princeton University]] and a doctoral degree in physics and geology from [[Caltech]] in 1972.<ref name=PU/> His PhD thesis concerned quarks.<ref>{{cite thesis |title=Quarks: currents and constituents |year=1973|url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/4807/|publisher=California Institute of Technology|doi=10.7907/102C-A509|access-date=September 16, 2020|last1=Melosh|first1=H. Jay|type=phd}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Quarks: Currents and constituents|year=1974|url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/4807/3/melosh-hj_1973.pdf|journal=Physical Review D|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.9.1095|access-date=September 16, 2020|last1=Melosh|first1=H. J.|volume=9|issue=4|pages=1095–1112|bibcode=1974PhRvD...9.1095M}}</ref>  Melosh's research interests include [[impact craters]], [[planetary tectonics]], and the physics of [[earthquakes]] and [[landslides]]. His recent research includes studies of the [[Giant-impact hypothesis|giant impact origin of the Moon]], the [[Chicxulub crater|Chicxulub impact]] that is thought to have extinguished most [[dinosaur]]s, and studies of ejection of rocks from their parent bodies. He was active in [[astrobiology|astrobiological]] studies that relate chiefly to the exchange of [[microorganisms]] between the terrestrial planets (a process known as [[panspermia]] or transpermia<ref>{{cite web |title=Swapping Rocks - Exchange of Surface Material Among the Planets |url=http://users.tpg.com.au/users/tps-seti/swaprock.html |publisher=Australian Spaceguard Survey |access-date=June 23, 2016 |archive-date=November 9, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201109130157/http://users.tpg.com.au/users/tps-seti/swaprock.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>).  

Melosh was a member of the [[American Geophysical Union]], [[Geological Society of America]], [[Meteoritical Society]], [[American Astronomical Society]] (Division of Planetary Sciences,) and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name=PU>{{cite web |title=Curriculum Vitae |url=http://www.eaps.purdue.edu/people/faculty-pages/vitae/melosh.pdf |publisher=Purdue University |access-date=June 24, 2016}}</ref> He was the recipient of the [[Barringer Medal]] of the [[Meteoritical Society]] for his work on the physics of impact, and of the [[G. K. Gilbert Award]] from the [[Geological Society of America]]. He was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 2003.<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060213020037/http://uanews.org/cgi-bin/WebObjects/UANews.woa/wa/MainStoryDetails?ArticleID=7267 U A News]}}</ref>

== Career ==
Melosh took his first faculty role at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] between 1976 and 1979, where he researched the Moon's orientation in relation to mass concentrations ([[Mass concentration (astronomy)|mascons]]) and large impacts, and was also a member of the [[GRAIL]] science team.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=In memory of H. Jay Melosh: Department of Physics and Astronomy: Purdue University |url=https://www.physics.purdue.edu/people/Tribute_Melosh.html |access-date=2025-02-12 |website=www.physics.purdue.edu}}</ref> He then went on to take a position with [[SUNY Stony brook|SUNY Stonybrook]] as an associate professor of geophysics until 1982 when he left to join the [[University of Arizona]] as a faculty member in the planetary sciences,<ref name=":0" /> where he continued work on impact cratering until 2009. In 2009, Dr. Melosh moved to the [[Purdue University]] Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences to study impact cratering, [[planetary science]], and geophysics until his retirement.<ref name=":0" />

==Awards and honors==
* Asteroid [[8216 Melosh]] is named in his honor.
* The American Geophysical Union 2008 Harry H. Hess Medal - for “outstanding achievements in research in the constitution and evolution of Earth and sister planets.”<ref>{{cite web |title=2008 Harry H. Hess Medal Winner |url=https://honors.agu.org/winners/h-jay-melosh/ |publisher=American Geophysical Union |access-date=June 23, 2016}}</ref>
* In 2024 Melosh Crater was named after him in his honor. The crater is located near the Aram Chaos terrain in the equatorial region of Mars. The crater is almost 100 km in diameter and has a history of lava infilling and water flooding.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Planetary Names |url=https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/16345?_ga=2.21699259.1093617626.1734711404-62101448.1696435020 |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=A legacy etched in the red planet: Mars crater named for planetary expert Jay Melosh - Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences - Purdue University |url=https://www.eaps.purdue.edu/news/articles/2024/1219_jaymeloshcrater.html |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=www.eaps.purdue.edu}}</ref>
